requirements:
R1. Implement in Rust as a SINGLE source file that compiles with rustc --edition 2024, std only. Output ONLY the Rust source code inside ```rust fences. Do not use inner attributes or inner documentation comments.

R2. Expose exactly these callable APIs (additional private helpers are allowed): pub fn encode_u64(value: u64) -> Vec<u8>; pub fn decode_u64(input: &[u8], start: usize) -> Result<(u64, usize), Error>; pub fn decode_many(input: &[u8], start: usize, count: usize) -> Result<(Vec<u64>, usize), Error>. The returned usize is the first unconsumed absolute input index.

R3. Define pub enum Error with variants StartOutOfBounds { offset: usize }, Truncated { offset: usize, start: usize }, Overflow { offset: usize, start: usize }. Error must derive Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq.

R4. Unsigned integers use little-endian base-128 (LEB128): seven payload bits per byte, bit 7 indicates another byte, least significant group first.

R5. encode_u64 emits the shortest representation, including [0] for zero, and never emits an empty vector.

R6. Values span the entire u64 domain, including u64::MAX; the longest valid representation has ten bytes.

R7. decode_u64 first validates start <= input.len(); otherwise return StartOutOfBounds { offset: start }, without examining input.

R8. Start equal to input.len() is a valid cursor, but decoding one integer there returns Truncated { offset: input.len(), start }.

R9. Decoding stops at the first byte whose continuation bit is clear and leaves any following bytes unread.

R10. At any missing byte before termination, return Truncated { offset: input.len(), start }, where start is the initial cursor of that integer.

R11. On byte ten (index start + 9), a payload greater than 1 is Overflow { offset: start + 9, start }, even if its continuation bit is clear.

R12. Any set continuation bit on byte ten is Overflow at that same byte, even when the input ends there; overflow takes precedence over truncation. Do not inspect an eleventh byte.

R13. Except for the ten-byte rules, decode accepts nonminimal encodings such as [0x80, 0] for zero and ten-byte zero encodings.

R14. decode_many decodes exactly count consecutive integers from start and returns their values in encounter order and the cursor after the last value.

R15. decode_many validates start before considering count, so an invalid start with count zero still returns StartOutOfBounds.

R16. With count zero and a valid start, decode_many returns an empty vector and the unchanged start, without reading bytes.

R17. When an integer in decode_many fails, return its error unchanged: its start is that integer's cursor, not the cursor of the batch. Return no partial vector.

R18. decode_many ignores trailing bytes after the requested count; an empty slice is valid only when count is zero. All functions must be deterministic and must not panic on any input slice or count (allocation exhaustion is outside the contract).
